idiom_name: Boost.Asio framing: length-prefixed sequence header plus a per-sequence std::map
implementation_notes: C++ has no messaging runtime, so the realization is a framing discipline plus receiver-side state: read the fixed sequence header with asio::async_read (a composed operation that loops over async_read_some until the buffer is full), then read exactly the declared payload, and keep one group entry per sequence identifier in a map keyed by that identifier with the parts stored by position. The alternative realization, cppzmq multipart messages, lets ZeroMQ deliver the ordered frames of one message atomically and is documented as a sibling variant; it removes position numbers inside a single message but not grouping across sends. The header-plus-map form remains the default because it works over any byte stream or broker.
pitfalls: A single async_read_some can complete short of the requested size; use the composed async_read for the header and the payload instead of a raw read.
Map entries for sequences that never complete are a leak: erase them on timeout and cap the number of live groups.
Serialise header fields in network byte order; raw struct writes differ between ABIs and compilers.

variants.name: ZeroMQ / cppzmq multipart messages
variants.implementation_notes: ZeroMQ delivers a multipart message as one atomic unit - frames arrive in order and are never interleaved with another message's frames - so a batch that fits one send needs no position numbers at all; use zmq::send_multipart / zmq::recv_multipart, or the sendmore flag on every part except the last, and keep a sequence identifier in the first frame when a batch spans several sends. Choose this when both ends already speak ZeroMQ; fall back to the header-plus-map form when the channel is a plain byte stream or a broker that reorders messages.
pitfalls: Multipart atomicity covers one send only: a sequence spread over several sends still needs position numbers and a release condition.
Receive with recv_multipart (or loop until the sendmore flag clears); polling for single frames loses the message boundary.
